docs.title: ats-strike
docs.text:
Turn a job description and your unstructured experiences into a tailored, two-page LaTeX CV and a cover letter, using any OpenAI-compatible model.

ats-strike is two halves that never share a machine by necessity:

  • a server that holds the model API keys, the prompts and the LaTeX toolchain, shipped as a container image;
  • a client that holds your CV data and your files, shipped as a single executable with no Python, no API key and no LaTeX of its own.

They speak HTTP, multipart/form-data in and JSON out, over a wire format both sides import and neither owns.

docs.title: The shape of a run
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    JD["a job posting<br/>(clipboard, folder or file)"] --> C["client<br/><i>your data, your files</i>"]
    C -->|HTTP| S["server<br/><i>models + pdflatex</i>"]
    S -->|"document · LaTeX · PDF · request ids"| C
    C --> OUT["CV/26-01-15/Acme_Corp_Head_of_IT/<br/>cv_you_head_of_it.pdf · .tex · .json<br/>analysis.json · job_description.txt · log.log"]

Your profile, your contact details and your images travel with each request and are thrown away when it ends. The server keeps no database and no accounts — only a directory per request, holding that request's log and, for a CV job, its state and its result.

docs.title: The pieces
docs.text:
ats-strike-client The CLI, a repository of its own. Watches your clipboard or a folder, keeps your CV data local, files every result in a dated folder. server/ The HTTP API. Writes the CV in six steps, validates it, compiles the PDF, analyses postings, writes letters. pipeline/ Everything that makes a CV — model calls, LaTeX — as a library the server calls. contracts/ The shapes both sides agree on — the one thing each side imports, so neither imports the other. The ats-strike-contract repository, as a submodule here and in the client.

ats-integration-tests holds all three repositories as submodules, and the tests that need the client and the server together.

The short quickstarts live in this repository's README.md and server/README.md, and in the client's client/README.md. These pages are the long form: what the system does, why it is built this way, and every parameter of both halves.

docs.title: CV pipeline v2: design
docs.text: Status: draft, 2026-11-12. The probe of section 11 has run: go, on the conditions listed there. Nothing of the build exists yet. This replaces the draft of 2026-11-10, which compiled the profile into facts and still wrote every CV with a model; section 12 says what was kept from it. When v2 ships, it replaces doc/cv-pipeline.md, which describes v1.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
v1 writes every CV from scratch: about 24 model calls and five minutes to rewrite duties that are, in most CVs, the same duties. The rewriting is where the errors come from (exaggeration, lost context, garbled sentences), and the keywords a job description asks for end up crammed into the summary.

v2 moves the writing out of the per-job path. Once per profile, the profile is compiled into a store: a tree of competences named in the market's words, and a pool of pre-written, reviewed bullets, each tagged with what it proves and how many lines it takes. For each job description, one model call places the job's requirements on the tree, and code selects the CV: which stories, at what length, in which experiences. A model then chooses between stored wordings, writes the headline and one summary sentence, and edits the job's own words in where the facts support them.

The balance between what a keyword search wants and what a reader wants is a set of weights sent with each request, so it can change without a redeploy.

A probe on one real profile and ten held-out job descriptions showed that the compiled pool can be trusted (4% of bullets wrong at the candidate's first reading), that the allocation is consistent (two runs share 83% of the placed importance), that the page budget holds in code (16 of 16 CVs fit at the first render), and that selection alone does not carry the job's words into the CV: literal coverage was 35% against v1's 62%, almost all of it the summary. So the varnish step's edits are part of the design, not a polish.

docs.title: 1. Why: what v1 does and what it costs
docs.text:
Measured on 51 CV runs of real applications, their 1,076 rendered bullets, and 2,547 unique job descriptions, all kept in a private data folder; then by the probe. Appendix A says how each number was counted.

Question Measured What it means Does v1 tailor the selection? Of 32 profile duties, 19 are in at least 70% of CVs, 7 are never shown, and 6 really vary. 47 of 51 CVs show the same 3 experiences. The scoring of every duty against every job buys little selection. Where do the job's keywords end up? Requirements with one of their keywords present, weighted by importance: 40% in the profile's own text, 58% in the CV, 40% in the CV without its summary. All of v1's keyword gain is the summary: 743 characters holding 7 of the job's keywords. The rewritten bullets add none. Can lines be budgeted in code? lines = ceil(characters / 98) is exact for 98.8% of bullets. In the probe, a line model in points put 16 of 16 CVs on two pages at the first render. Yes. The render is a check, not a loop. Are bullet lengths varied? 94% of bullets are exactly 2 lines, at a median 156 of 196 characters. No variety, and about a fifth of the bullet area is blank. What does a CV cost? v1: a median 24 calls, 290 seconds and 221,000 tokens, 63% of them thinking. v2 in the probe: 5 to 6 calls per CV, about 30 once per profile. Is a job's vocabulary predictable? 1,796 distinct keywords in 51 jobs; 77% occur in one job only. A job's wording cannot be written into the bullets in advance. How much of a job can the profile not prove? v1: about 25% of a job's importance has no duty that proves it. v2: 18% of importance lands on ghost leaves, 0.3% nowhere. This is the ceiling of any keyword score, and it has to be reported. Is relevance literal? Of v1's 1,098 strong matches between a duty and a requirement, 17% have one of the requirement's keywords in the duty. Matching is mostly a judgment of meaning. Keyword matching alone cannot select. Can a one-time compile be trusted? 4.0% of 176 pool bullets wrong at the candidate's first reading; the review edited 12% of lines. Yes. Bullets need no validation per job. Does selection carry the job's words? Literal coverage 35% against v1's 62%; summary alone 19% against 53%. No. The varnish must put them in.

docs.title: 2. Goals and non-goals
docs.text:
Goals:

  1. Write once, select many times. The text of a CV is written and reviewed once per profile, not once per job.
  2. A tunable balance. Keyword coverage against context, stories and a complete career, as weights in the client's configuration.
  3. No silent gaps. An experience is left out only when the balance says so, and the earliest and the most recent are always shown.
  4. A readable summary. The job's keywords move to where they cost a reader least.
  5. Fewer moving parts per job: 5 to 6 calls instead of 24.

Non-goals:

  • The LaTeX render, the letter, JD detection and analysis, the sessions and the event stream stay as they are.
  • No rules on metric density, bullet formulas or action verbs.
  • No external skills taxonomy. The tree is built from the profile and from what real job descriptions ask.
  • Nothing personal is stored on the server.

docs.title: 3. The design at a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    PROF(["candidate_profile.json"]) -->|"once per profile version"| ITEMS["<b>items</b><br/>base items and stories"]
    JDS(["a sample of job descriptions"]) --> TREE
    ITEMS --> TREE["<b>tree</b><br/>competences, market names, aliases"]
    TREE --> POOL["<b>pool</b><br/>bullets on a ladder, groups,<br/>skill phrases, summary frames"]
    POOL --> REV["<b>review</b><br/>code checks, a pool review, the candidate"]
    REV --> STORE(["the store<br/>next to the profile, editable"])
    STORE --> START(["POST /v1/cv<br/>JD + profile + store + mix"])
    START --> ALLOC["<b>allocate</b><br/>the job's requirements onto the tree"]
    ALLOC --> SEL["select<br/>(code) content and length"]
    SEL --> FIT{"over the page limit?"}
    FIT -->|"yes"| DOWN["step a story down a rung,<br/>then remove"] --> FIT
    FIT -->|"no"| VAR["<b>varnish</b><br/>wording, the job's words,<br/>headline"]
    VAR --> HL["highlight<br/>(code)"]
    HL --> FIN(["result"])

Terms used below:

  • base item: one statement from the profile, typed context, action or result.
  • story: the base items that tell one piece of work together.
  • node: one competence in the tree. A leaf is something a recruiter searches for. A ghost leaf is one the profile cannot prove.
  • rung: one length of a story's bullet: 1, 2 or 3 lines.
  • wording: one of the stored versions of a rung.
  • group: bullets that go into the CV together or not at all.
  • slot: one place in a planned CV, to be filled by a wording.
  • mix: the weights that balance the keyword score against the human score.

docs.title: 4. The store: once per profile
docs.text:
The store is compiled from the profile, kept next to it on the client, and editable by hand. It is personal data: it travels with each CV request, as the profile does, and the server keeps none of it.

For the probe's profile (five experiences) the store came to 120 items in 27 stories, a tree of 176 nodes, and a pool of 162 bullets, 5 compact lines, 5 role summaries, 39 skill phrases and 5 summary frames. Compiling it took about 30 model calls.

docs.title: 4.1 Base items and stories
docs.text:
Each experience's duties are cut into numbered base items. From the fictional candidate in examples/candidate:

{"id": "e1.i21", "experience": 1, "story": "e1.s6", "type": "action",
 "text": "Defined and documented the backup and restore procedures and the disaster recovery plan.",
 "source": ["Defined and documented the backup and restore procedures and the disaster recovery plan"],
 "agency": "did", "tags": ["disaster recovery", "operational procedures"]}
  • source is copied verbatim from the profile. Code checks that each span is a substring of its experience and drops an item that fails. In the probe the spans covered 93–97% of each experience's duty text and no item was dropped.
  • type drives repetition. Two bullets never share an action or a result; a context may recur, spelled out once.
  • agency is led, did or supported, with what the profile's notes say about scope. "I guided my team, NOT the rehearsals" stays attached to the rehearsal item.
  • References between duties ("the cloud projects above") are resolved, so each item stands alone.
  • Context belongs to the experience, not to a story. Job-level context (the system, the client, the team) is kept at the experience level and handed to every pool call. The probe first put it in stories of its own, and the bullets of a call that was not handed it came out bare.
  • A story is one system and one phase of work, not one duty of the profile. The candidate found the probe's stories "a bit granular" and merged five into two; the profile's duty split is not the unit.

docs.title: 4.2 The competence tree
docs.text:
One tree, three levels, numbered: disciplines, competences, and leaves. A job's requirements are later placed on this same tree, so a general requirement lands on a competence and a specific one on a leaf.

It is built in this order:

  1. Collect what the market asks. Run the existing jd_evaluation on a sample of job descriptions, spread over role families and languages.
  2. Tag what the profile proves. Each base item gets competence tags.
  3. Join them. A model drafts the tree from both lists. Each node takes the market's most frequent name and lists its aliases ("Kubernetes", "K8s"). A broad node asked in many phrasings, such as stakeholder management, is split along the distinctions jobs make. A leaf nobody asks for sits under a parent that is asked for.
  4. Attach the items. A second call gives each action or result item the leaves it proves, at three levels: touches, a substantial part, is the work. A context item attaches at the first level at most: a leaf that only the situation supports ("the team worked in Agile") is weakly proven, enough for the varnish to use the word in a bullet carrying that context, never enough for a skill phrase.
  5. Add ghost leaves: the most-asked things the profile cannot prove. A requirement can then land precisely as a gap.
  6. The candidate reviews it. Numbering is then frozen; new nodes are appended.
  7. Test it on jobs it was not built from: how much importance lands on a proven node, on a ghost, or nowhere.

What the probe taught about the tree:

  • proven must rest on more than one weak attachment. Two attach calls on the same tree agreed on every level-3 pair, but six leaves flipped between proven and ghost because each hung on a single level-1 or level-2 item. A leaf is proven by two calls, or the candidate checks every leaf with one weak item.
  • Some ghosts are attachment misses. Two operating-system leaves took importance as ghosts while a story is mixed-OS administration. The held-out test lists the ghosts an item plausibly proves.
  • Aliases need their own check. About 20 nodes came with aliases that are a narrower thing, a broader thing or another product, against an explicit rule. Each node keeps two lists: what is the same thing, and what counts as it. Only the first may ever replace printed words.
  • Compound names hide the plain term. A node called "DevOps & CI/CD" never occurs literally in a job or a bullet; the plain term is the name or an alias.
  • Fixed sections prove too. Languages, certifications and the skills list are not items; a leaf they prove carries an outside note and counts.
  • Placement is loosest where the tree is coarse: the job furthest from the profile's centre had the lowest agreement between two allocations (66%). The corpus sample is where the margins get detail.

The tree's names and aliases are also what gets printed in the skills block and in the summary's keyword slot. That is why the naming matters.

docs.title: 4.3 The pool
docs.text:
• Bullets on a ladder. Each story is written at 1, 2 and 3 lines, to the line grid, and each rung in 2 or 3 wordings. For the disaster recovery story of the example candidate:
Rung Text 1 line Wrote the disaster recovery plan of the Games' results system against a 2-hour RTO. 2 lines Wrote the backup, restore and disaster recovery procedures of the Games' results system, a core system with a 2-hour RTO. My team tested them at the full-scale rehearsals and met the SLA.
  • Groups. A longer story told over two or three bullets, or bullets that refer to each other, form a group. It is selected, placed and trimmed as one unit, so no bullet ever refers to one that was cut. Up to 7 lines; a story that joins several pieces of work, up to 9. The candidate's verdict on the probe: "I do love the groups".
  • The role summary comes first. It is written before the ladder and handed to the ladder call, so a bullet carries only the context the header and the role summary do not. Five of the candidate's thirteen notes on the probe's pool were bullets repeating what the header or the role summary already said.
  • Compact lines. One line per experience, dense with terms, for a job shown only to keep the career whole.
  • Skill phrases, composed where it helps: "Terraform IaC", "CI/CD with Jenkins". A phrase needs a leaf proven at level 3, or by two items: the two wrong phrases of the probe each rested on one weak attachment.
  • Summary frames, one per role family: pre-written text with <<job_title>>, a slot for a few keywords, and a slot for one <<sentence>>. They were the weakest pieces of the probe's pool, written far from the items: their numbers and years are checked in code against the profile, and they are reviewed at compile time.

Each bullet and group carries: the items it uses and those it fully covers, its nodes and how fully it proves each, its line count, the terms it contains, and two human factors scored once, from 0 to 2: context and success.

docs.title: 4.4 Review
docs.text:
Code checks first: length against the rung, every number present in the items, "led" or "managed" only where an item's agency says so, no bullet made of context alone, group size. Then a model reviews each experience's pool against the profile, with minimal edits. Then the candidate reads the pool, marking each piece ok, taste or wrong, with a note; the marked file is the store's editing loop, and a marked bullet is rewritten from the note.

Two rules the probe forced:

  • The pool review has its own prompt. v1's review, shown one story's ladder alone, read the wordings and rungs as repetitions and replaced 7 of 23 bullets with other stories' facts. Shown the whole experience, told that a story's bullets are alternatives of which one is printed, and allowed to edit only the new pieces, it behaved.
  • An edit that breaks the line limit is refused. One review edit took a three-line bullet to four.

The review edited 12% of the probe's lines, mostly exaggerations ("led" for a part of the work, "eliminated" for "saved"). It is not consistent across wordings and missed exaggerations the candidate caught, so the candidate's reading stays the last check. It is sized for a quarter of an hour at a time.

The catalog the evaluation's judge uses stays out of this step: a generator tuned on its grader cannot be graded by it.

Every bullet is keyed to its source items, so a profile change regenerates only what it touches, and a hand-edited bullet is locked.

docs.title: 5.1 Allocate
docs.text:
One model call, about a minute. It extracts the job's requirements as jd_evaluation does today, each with its importance, and places each on the tree:

{"name": "Container orchestration in production", "importance": 80,
 "terms": ["Kubernetes"], "node": "3.2.1", "relation": "same"}
Relation Meaning Points on the node same, broader the node is what is asked, or the job asks more generally importance narrower the job asks something more specific than the node half sibling the node is a ghost leaf (code labels this; the model is not told which leaves are ghosts) importance, on the ghost none nothing in the tree none; the requirement is reported as unmatched

Points flow up at half per level, and what a node inherits is capped at its largest single contribution, so a discipline and its own skills do not count twice.

The job's literal terms are the requirement's keywords in English, as jd_evaluation returns them, plus the job's own words when the text has them. The probe counted only words found in the job text, which left the selector blind to every requirement of a job written in Italian (six of the ten) while the measurement counted them. A same term the tree did not know comes back as a pending alias for the store; the probe produced 47 in ten jobs, too many to apply unreviewed.

docs.title: 5.2 Select
docs.text:
Pure code, about two seconds. It decides what is said and how many lines it takes, for the whole CV at once:

  • which stories, at which rung, or as a group;
  • which experiences are shown in full, in compact form, or not at all. The earliest and the most recent are always shown;
  • the 10 skill phrases, on 2 lines, taken by the job's terms they add;
  • the summary frame and the terms for its keyword slot.

It starts from the two mandatory experiences in compact form and repeatedly takes the move with the best gain per line under the objective of section 6: add a story, step one up a rung, open an experience with its two best slots at any rung, add one in compact form. It goes on with the least-loss move while one fits, so the page is filled; then a refill pass drops the weakest slot and runs again, keeping the result if it scores higher. Inside a job, bullets go most relevant first, except that a story introducing the job's system comes before stories that assume it.

Each of the first three rules is a correction from the probe: a stop-at-no-gain rule left one CV at 31 of 71 lines; opening an experience with two one-line bullets kept a core experience compact in 6 of 10 CVs; and the greedy is path-dependent, so one job scored lower on the keyword score at a higher keyword weight.

docs.title: 5.3 Render and fit
docs.text: The plan is rendered and its pages counted. While it runs over the limit, a story steps down a rung, or a group becomes its single bullet; only when no story can step down is something removed. The line model is in points, calibrated from two renders and one check of the template: the line pitch, the gap between items (a third of a line each), the header of a full and of a compact experience. In the probe it put 16 of 16 CVs on two pages at the first render, with one to four lines to spare.

docs.title: 5.4 Varnish
docs.text:
A model reads the assembled CV as a whole and:

  • puts the job's words in, in the summary first and then in the bullets, through the existing replace_in_* tools. Code refuses an edit that adds a number, a technology or a line, and the existing validation prompt checks the result. This is the step the probe made mandatory: selection alone reached 35% literal coverage against v1's 62%, and the body review rightly strips terms the profile does not back;
  • picks one stored wording per slot, for varied openers, rhythm and the job's words;
  • flags two slots that tell the same fact; code replaces one with the selector's next candidate. Shared context is not a repeat: that was every flag the probe raised;
  • regenerates a bullet it cannot use, in three tiers: a tool returns the story's other stored bullets with the same line count; failing that, a small local edit (a reference the role summary already explains, "the" for a thing not yet introduced), saved and applied at once, checked for its line count; failing that, a new sentence from a model that sees the profile, the pool, the story, the requested edit and the scores, which waits for the candidate's approval before it joins the pool. The last tier comes last in the build.

A separate call writes the headline and the summary's one sentence. The headline is the job's title when the profile's titles license it; otherwise it is written from the job, the experiences shown and the allowed titles. In the probe every headline stayed within the titles held or allowed.

The model chooses between reviewed sentences, so it cannot exaggerate or garble. Code checks each reply and falls back to a default wording, so a failed call still yields a CV.

docs.title: 5.5 Highlight
docs.text: In code, from spans marked in the pool: the job's terms in bold, heaviest first, a few per CV, taken from the allocation's English keywords (the job's own words gave an Italian job none).

docs.title: 6. Scoring and the mix
docs.text:
The keyword score is measured against everything the job asks, unmatched requirements included. It has two parts:

  • literal: a first occurrence of any of a requirement's terms counts its weight in full, a second occurrence a third more;
  • proof: per node, the best piece counts in full, the next a third, the next a fifth, capped at one. A compact line is a piece.

The divisors 1, 3, 5 make covering a new requirement worth more than repeating one, and give each requirement a share of the CV close to its share of the job [2]. A sum of this shape is monotone submodular, the class for which greedy selection under a budget is the standard method [1].

The human score has five terms:

Term Counted from continuity each experience left out costs its share of the career's years completeness the action and result items the CV covers, over the whole career rhythm the mix of 1-, 2- and 3-line bullets context the pre-scored context of the chosen bullets success their pre-scored success

The first three are counted in code on the selection. The last two are judged once per bullet when the pool is compiled, where the candidate can read and correct them. Nothing is judged per job: a model scoring on a fine scale is inconsistent from one call to the next [3], and v1's scores were multiples of 5 in 99.9% of cases.

The mix is a table in the client's cv.toml, sent with each request as pages already is:

[mix]
ats = 0.5           # 0 = human only, 1 = keyword score only
literal = 0.5       # inside the keyword score: the job's own words against proven coverage
continuity = 1.0    # the human terms, relative to each other
completeness = 1.0
context = 1.0
success = 1.0
rhythm = 0.5

In the probe the human score stayed within 0.04 across every plan and every mix, so the lever moved the CV little: context and success as means penalize every added bullet. The weights stay internal until the evaluation shows they matter, and the two pre-scored terms are to be reworked as page-normalized sums.

docs.title: 7. What gets deleted
docs.text:
• profile_scoring and the |3-80,7-40 score suffixes.
  • format_selection and the formats.
  • The per-experience writers and their validation rounds.
  • The highlight call.
  • capped_coverage.
  • The two meta requirements added to every job, "success stories" and "concrete examples": they become the pool's success and context scores.

docs.title: 8. How v2 keeps the house rules
docs.text:
• The pipeline is a library. Points, selection, fit and highlight are pure functions of values. The store arrives with the request.
  • No hidden global state. The mix and the page geometry are arguments.
  • Contracts. The store gets a pydantic model in cv_contracts.
  • Tests. The pure functions get unit tests on hand-made values; the graph test keeps the fake HTTP client inside a real ModelSelector; the golden render stays.

docs.title: 9. Evaluation
docs.text:
• Thorough runs decide, v1 against v2, on the same day with the same judge. Literal coverage is scored on both v1's key points and v2's allocation.
  • New columns in the evaluation, checked in code on any CV: pages, the career span shown, the headline against the job's title, the summary's length, and bullets that refer to another bullet outside a group. Each is a feature that changed when v1 replaced the pipeline before it: CVs showing the whole career fell from 62% to 6%, headlines naming the job's kind of role from 66% to 36%, the summary grew from 528 to 734 characters, and bullets referring to another rose from 0.2% to 1.9%. v2 passes most of these by construction, so they guard against regressions more than they measure progress.
  • The human score has no ground truth beyond the candidate's own reading. Three checks, in this order: blind pairwise reading of CVs built at different mixes, which also sets the weights; a direction check on CVs already sent, where the score should rate the set that did better in practice above the other; and the evaluation's readability and style columns, which stay independent of the pipeline. The probe could do only three blind pairs (v2 preferred in two); the rest is the evaluation's, in short sessions.
  • Similarity between the CV and the job stays an evaluation column. In the probe, the tree's top-eight stories fell four to eight inside the stories the selector chose, an embedding ranking three to seven; nothing says which is right until the candidate's own picks are measured.

docs.title: 10. Risks
docs.text: Risk Mitigation An unusual job gets generic bullets: the pool cannot reframe a story for a requirement nobody anticipated the varnish's regeneration tiers; the unmatched report shows when it happens The job's words stay out: selection alone reached 35% literal coverage the varnish's edits are on the critical path, and the evaluation scores coverage on both key-point sets The tree's abstract nodes do not discriminate, and a leaf on one weak item flips split along the distinctions jobs make; proven by two calls or the candidate's check A wrong alias prints a false claim two alias lists per node; only "same thing" may replace words, and a new alias waits for review The review misses what the candidate catches the candidate's reading is the last check, sized for a quarter of an hour The scores are proxies with no outcome data behind them few weights, kept internal until the evaluation shows they move the CV A client's own template has its own geometry the line constants are calibrated from the template; the render stays the judge

docs.title: 11. Plan of work
docs.text:
The probe ran first, with no repository change, in a git-ignored scratch folder on the private data: items, tree and pool for one real profile; ten held-out job descriptions allocated twice, selected, varnished and rendered; the candidate reviewed the items and tree, the whole pool, and three blind pairs against v1.

Criterion Result G1 the candidate marks at most 5% of the pool's bullets as wrong pass: 4.0% at the first reading, 1.2% after one rewrite G2 two allocations share at least 80% of their points; at most 10% of importance lands nowhere pass: 83%; 0.3% nowhere G3 keyword coverage at least v1's, with a summary under 500 characters and 10 skills on 2 lines fail: 35% against 62%; the summary and skills limits held G4 two pages with the earliest and the most recent job; the first render fits in 8 of 10 pass: 16 of 16 at the first render G5 the candidate prefers the new CV in at least 7 of 10 blind pairs direction only: 2 of 3; ten pairs were too many to read

Go, on four conditions: the varnish puts the job's words in (G3); the selector fills the page, opens experiences with their best slots and counts completeness over the whole career; the pool review has its own prompt; context sits at the experience level.

Then the build, one sub-plan each:

Sub-plan Output S1 Base items and stories the decomposition prompt, the source check, item types; context at the experience level; stories by system and phase S2 Competence tree the corpus sample, the shape and attach prompts, proven on more than one weak attachment, the alias check, ghost leaves, the held-out test S3 Pool role summary first, ladder, wordings, groups, compact lines, skill phrases on strong leaves, summary frames with checks, pre-scores S4 Review and store the pool review prompt, edits refused over the limit, the marking loop, file format, lock rules, the compile endpoint and client command S5 Allocation the prompt, relations, point rules, English literal terms, the unmatched report, pending aliases S6 Selector and scores the objective, the mix, fill and refill, bullet order, the plan report S7 Geometry and render line constants from calibration; compact experience and skills block in the template S8 Varnish the job's words in, the pick, the repeat check, regeneration tiers one and two, headline and sentence S9 Highlight marked spans, rules in code S10 Protocol, client, deletion of v1 request parts, the mix, artifacts, docs S11 Evaluation the new columns; a thorough run of v1 against v2; the reading checks in short sessions S12 Regeneration, tier three a new sentence written on demand

The wire changes (a compile endpoint, the store and the mix as request parts, the model roles) are decided in S4 and S10. v2 is 2.0.0.

docs.title: 12. Alternatives considered
docs.text:
• Writing each CV from compiled facts (the draft of 2026-11-10). It fixed the units but kept a writer and a verifier in every CV, which is where v1's errors and cost are. Kept from it: facts and stories, the diminishing coverage objective, header costs instead of formats, highlight in code, and the fit rule.
  • Validating every bullet per job. The probe showed it is not needed: 4% of pool bullets were wrong at the candidate's first reading, and the review loop plus the candidate's marks brought it to about 1%.
  • A tree per job description, matched to the candidate's. Aligning two trees is noisier than placing each requirement on a fixed one, and jd_evaluation already overlaps with itself by only about half from run to run.
  • Similarity of bullets to the job as the selector. It knows no importance, says "similar" rather than "proves", and has no diminishing returns, so the bullets nearest the job are near-duplicates of each other. It is also what the evaluation measures.
  • Swapping aliases for the job's words in code. It never fired in the probe (0 swaps in 16 CVs), and with the aliases as the model wrote them it would have swapped one product for another. The model's guarded edits do the job.
  • A model choosing the content. format_selection chose the same format in about 96% of its decisions until its prompt was rebalanced.
  • Code choosing the wording. Code cannot judge how a page reads.
  • A long skills list as the keyword carrier. Rejected for the reader: 10 items on 2 lines.
  • A summary written whole per job, or pre-written whole. The first is what gets stuffed; the second carries none of the job's words. Frames with slots sit between them, and the varnish edits the job's words into the frame.
  • A hard rule against career gaps. An irrelevant job may be left out; it costs in proportion to its length.

docs.title: 13. Open questions
docs.text:
1. Bullet order. Most relevant first, or the story that explains the job's system first? The probe tried the former with one exception rule.
  2. Allocation. One call that extracts and places (the probe's choice), or two?
  3. Similarity. A selection term with its own weight, a check on the allocation, or evaluation only?
  4. Geometry. Constants in the client's configuration, or measured from a calibration render of the template (the probe's choice)?
  5. The human terms. Means, sums normalized by the page, or something that moves the CV when the mix moves?

docs.title: Appendix A: how the numbers were measured
docs.text:
All from the artifacts each v1 run stores under steps/, the rendered PDFs and the job descriptions in the private data folder; the probe's numbers from its own outputs in a git-ignored folder. The scripts were throwaway; these are the counting rules.

  • Selection. A CV duty maps to the profile duty of the same experience with the same score suffix. A duty's rate is the share of runs that show it, over duties present in at least 10 runs.
  • Keywords. For each run, the requirements of key_points.json without the two meta items. A requirement counts when one of its keywords occurs as a whole word, ignoring case, in the text measured: the profile, the final CV, or the CV without its summary. Shares are weighted by importance and averaged over runs. The probe scored its CVs by the same rule, on v1's key points of the same ten jobs and on its own allocation's keywords.
  • Lines. Each bullet of the final document is matched to its lines in the PDF's text layout. The model ceil(characters / 98) is compared with the count. The probe's line model in points was calibrated from the text positions of two renders.
  • Cost. The last line of each run's log; for the probe, one line per model request.
  • Vocabulary. Keywords of all requirements, lower-cased.
  • Unproven demand. The importance of requirements whose best duty score is under 40, over the run's total; for the probe, the importance landing on ghost leaves or on no node.
  • Literal against judged matches. For each match scored 60 or more, whether any keyword of its requirement occurs in the duty.
  • Market terms. Regular expressions, in English and Italian, over the unique job descriptions.
  • Pool quality. The candidate marked every bullet ok, taste or wrong; the wrong share is over all bullets. Review edits are counted per line.
  • Allocation consistency. The two runs' point vectors, after the flow upward, normalized; the shared mass is the sum of the minimum per node.

docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph your["your machine"]

        OUT["CV/ · discarded/ · error/ · working/<br/>applications.xlsx"]

        CLI --> OUT
    end

    subgraph wire["contracts"]
        CT["cv_contracts<br/>Envelope · StoreItem · Status · Done · Failure<br/>ServerStatus · Analysed · Rendered · Letter<br/>PROTOCOL · static_jd_guess"]
    end

    subgraph host["wherever you run it (one per server version)"]
        API["<b>cv_server</b><br/>the protocol: FastAPI, pack reader,<br/>sessions, SSE"]
        PIPE["<b>cv_pipeline</b><br/>facade · pack · jd_validator · cv_generator (LangGraph)<br/>cv_review · cv_renderer · letter_generator"]
        RES["resources<br/>prompts · schemas · resume.tex.jinja<br/>models.toml"]
        STORE["ATS_WORK_DIR<br/>one session per CV job"]
        API --> PIPE
        RES --> PIPE
        API --> STORE
    end

    PROV["OpenAI-compatible<br/>/chat/completions"]
    TEX["pdflatex"]

    CLI -->|"multipart: pack · job · settings"| API
    API -->|"JSON envelope<br/>CV: server-sent events"| CLI
    CLI -.imports.-> CT
    API -.imports.-> CT
    PIPE --> PROV
    PIPE --> TEX

client → contracts ← server → pipeline. The client and the server live in separate repositories and never import each other, the pipeline imports none of the others and knows no HTTP, and the server reaches the pipeline only through its top level (from cv_pipeline import ...); tests/test_architecture.py, here and in the client's repository, fails the build if any of that breaks. The contracts package depends on pydantic and nothing else: it is loaded both by a web server and by a frozen executable, and has to stay cheap in both.

Package Holds Ships as client/ Your server folders — profile, contact data, template, images — the output tree, the spreadsheet A PyInstaller executable, ~1 file, from its own repository, ats-strike-client server/ The protocol: request reading, auth, sessions, the event stream Inside the container image pipeline/ Everything that makes a CV: the prompts and schemas, the models and their API keys, the LaTeX template and toolchain Inside the container image, ~780 MB with TeX contracts/ The wire format: the envelope, the payloads, a thing to store, the protocol number, the free JD pre-check A pydantic-only package with its own repository, ats-strike-contract, checked out here as a git submodule

The wire knows no pipeline: the client sends a pack — every file of a server folder — and stores what the server tells it to store. So one client talks to a 0.5, a 1.x and a 2.0 server, side by side on one posting, and contracts/ is the same submodule and server/src the same files on every release line; only pipeline/ differs. See the protocol.

docs.title: What crosses the wire
docs.text:
Everything personal arrives with the request, in the pack. The server has no database, no accounts and no seeded state; the only thing it keeps is a CV job's session, one directory of events:

$ATS_WORK_DIR/<session id>/events/
    000001.json   {"type": "status", "data": {"status": "started", ...}}
    000002.json   {"type": "store", "data": {"type": "log", ...}}       a log line
    000003.json   {"type": "store", "data": {"type": "step", ...}}      a step's result
    ...
    000041.json   {"type": "store", "data": {"type": "cv", ...}}        the PDF
    000042.json   {"type": "done", "data": {...}}                       the last event

Each event is its own file, written once and never changed — which is what a bucket mounted as a folder (OSS, Cloud Storage) can do: an object there cannot be appended to, and a rename is a copy. A reader lists the directory and reads what is new; the one file that may not read whole yet is the newest, so a reader stops there and finds it complete on its next look. The session id is the client's: the SHA-256 of the posting's text, so the same posting finds its session again. A session is deleted when the client acknowledges it, or once its last event is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS; a running one, never. The scratch directory a job compiles in is on local disk, and is gone with the job.

docs.title: Inside the server
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    REQ["request"] --> MW["RequestContextMiddleware<br/>assigns request_id, binds the Run"]
    MW --> AUTH{"ATS_API_TOKEN set?"}
    AUTH -->|"no match"| E401["401 unauthorized"]
    AUTH -->|"ok / not set"| PARTS["read_request<br/>pack · job · settings<br/>names, ≤200 files, size, JSON object"]
    PARTS --> SLOT{"a free job slot?"}
    SLOT -->|"no"| E429["429 too_many_jobs<br/>Retry-After: 30"]
    SLOT -->|"yes"| KIND{"which endpoint?"}
    KIND -->|"/v1/jd/*, /v1/letter, /v1/cv/render"| POOL["threadpool<br/>answer when done"]
    KIND -->|"/v1/cv"| THREAD["worker thread<br/>answer 202 now"]
    POOL --> ENV["Envelope<br/>with its log lines as items"]
    THREAD --> EVENTS["a status per step, a store per<br/>step result, log line and the CV"]
    EVENTS --> STREAM["GET /v1/cv/{id}/events"]

POST /v1/cv for a session id that already has one skips the slot and the thread: it answers 202 with reattached: true, and the caller follows the events that are there.

  • One exception handler. describe_failure() is the single place that decides what an exception produces on the wire, so a failure body has the same shape as a success: a request_id, ok: false and one line naming the kind and the stage. See error model.
  • One semaphore. ATS_MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS (10) bounds requests in flight. A full server refuses immediately rather than queueing a caller for minutes.
  • The pipeline is a library. cv_pipeline takes the pack, the job and the settings in memory and returns values, or hands its outputs to a sink; it resolves no paths and writes nothing outside the scratch directory it is handed. Its face is Pipeline (detect, analyze, letter, cv, render, info), and every expected failure leaves it as a PipelineError with a kind. The server reads models.toml and the environment through Pipeline.build(), once at startup. That is what makes it safe to run per request.
  • The LaTeX subprocess is sandboxed. Shell escape off, reads and writes confined to the scratch directory, no stdin, a timeout, its own HOME and TEXMFVAR. A request may supply both the template and a whole .tex, so both are treated as hostile input.

docs.title: The models
docs.text:
One provider, one API key, one endpoint — declared once in the [provider] table of pipeline/resources/models.toml. Every role calls it, except a role that sets use_alternate_provider = N (N ≥ 2), which calls provider N instead — the [provider] variable names with N appended (MODEL_API_KEY2 / MODEL_BASE_URL2 for 2):

Role Used for Shipped as detect JD detection: a one-word YES/NO on text that passed the free checks deepseek-v4.1-flash, thinking off, 1000 max output tokens, temperature 0 analysis JD analysis; searches the web for distances and company facts qwen3.8-flash, thinking on, max effort letter Cover letters; searches the web for the employer qwen3.8-flash, thinking on, max effort jd_evaluation A CV's first step: the JD's key points, each with an importance deepseek-flash on DeepSeek's API (provider 2), medium effort profile_scoring Each list of the profile scored against the key points the same, high effort format_selection The CV format, the experiences shown and their duty caps the same, medium effort cv Writing the CV body, and each experience on its own the same, medium effort validation Checking the body and each experience against the profile, as replace_in_* tool calls the same, medium effort highlight The **bold**/*italic* keyword pass over the validated CV the same, medium effort

See the CV pipeline for how the last six fit together.

Every call goes through cv_pipeline.models: one LangChain chat model per role, built once at startup by the role's model_provider (standard, on ChatOpenAI, or deepseek, on ChatDeepSeek), and two methods. ModelSelector.call_llm(role, type, system_prompt, messages) returns the reply as a pydantic model, a bool (YES/NO), a str, or a JSON list or dict; call_tools(role, tool, …) returns the arguments of the tool calls the reply made. Both retry a reply that is empty, cut off or invalid — three calls in all, each retry told what was wrong. Provider-specific request fields (thinking_budget, enable_search) are the role's extra_body, sent as given: nothing checks a combination against what the endpoint supports. Any key of a role can be overridden with a ATS_<ROLE>_<FIELD> environment variable without editing the file; an empty value drops the key. A request's settings can bring an extra_body for every role but detect, which supersedes all of that role's settings for that request.

Every pydantic reply is validated. Its schema reaches the model once: in the request with json_schema, in the system prompt with json_mode. A weak mode costs a retry, never correctness. The CV steps reply with JSON their prompts describe — the writer's two schemas are part of its input — and are parsed, not validated.

docs.title: Asynchrony, and why
docs.text:
Writing a CV takes minutes. POST /v1/cv answers 202 and hands the work to a plain thread that outlives the response; the thread reports itself by appending events to the session, and GET /v1/cv/{id}/events streams them — everything so far, then each new one, until the last. A stream is a reader of files, so it can be opened again at any time: after a dropped connection, with Last-Event-ID, to get what it missed; after a client crash, from the start. The client acknowledges the session (DELETE) only once everything it streamed is stored.

The consequences are worth knowing before you deploy:

  • A running job lives in one instance. Its events are files, so any instance sharing the work root can replay them, but only the instance that started it is writing them. Run one instance.
  • WEB_CONCURRENCY=1. The slots and the workers are per-process, and a starting process ends every session that has not ended with a 503 error — correct for its own orphans, wrong for a sibling's live jobs.
  • A job cannot be cancelled yet. An abandoned one holds a slot until its own budget runs out (ATS_REQUEST_BUDGET_SECONDS, 20 minutes, read by the pipeline), and its session cannot be acknowledged until then.

docs.title: Observability
docs.text:
Every response carries a request_id, and so does the X-Request-Id header. Every line the server logs to stdout carries it too.

A CV job streams its own account as things to store: every line it logged — one per model call with its duration and token counts — each step's result, and, as the last log line before the last event, the run's total — failed attempts included, because they were paid for. An analysis, a letter or a render reply carries its log lines the same way, as items. The client writes the lines into log.log under the server's name, and each result into that server's subfolder of the job.

docs.title: Building the server
docs.text: The server is a container image: a Python virtualenv, the LaTeX toolchain and uvicorn. It mounts nothing and seeds nothing.

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
cd <repo root>
DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 docker build -t ats-strike-server .

The Dockerfile lives at the repository root, not in server/, because some cloud builders refuse a Dockerfile in a subfolder. The build context is the root: the image needs contracts/ and server/, and nothing else.

Classic builder only. No BuildKit features and no heredocs — CI builds with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0 on purpose, and the image must stay buildable that way.

flowchart TB
    subgraph s1["stage 1 — build (uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim)"]
        L1["pyproject.toml · uv.lock<br/>+ the three member pyprojects"] --> L2["uv sync --frozen --no-dev<br/>--package ats-strike-server<br/>--no-install-workspace"]
        L2 --> L3["contracts/src · pipeline/src · pipeline/resources · server/src"]
        L3 --> L4["uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-editable<br/>→ /app/.venv"]
    end
    subgraph s2["stage 2 — runtime (python:3.12-slim-bookworm)"]
        R1["texlive-latex-base + texlive-fonts-recommended + cm-super"] --> R2["vendored fontawesome5<br/>→ TEXMFLOCAL"]
        R2 --> R3["COPY --from=build /app/.venv"]
        R3 --> R4["entrypoint.sh → ats-strike"]
    end
    L4 --> R3

Why the layers are in that order: the lock file changes rarely and the code changes every commit, so dependencies resolve in a layer of their own. --no-editable copies the packages into the venv instead of linking them back to /app/src, so the runtime stage needs nothing but the venv.

docs.title: What the LaTeX bits are for
docs.text:
Package Why texlive-latex-base hyperref, graphicx, array, hhline, amsmath, babel-english — everything resume.tex.jinja uses texlive-fonts-recommended The font files behind psnfss (Charter, Times, Palatino, ...). The stock template does not need them; a template of your own that loads \usepackage{charter} does cm-super Type 1 CM fonts. Without them, T1 encoding falls back to bitmap fonts and the PDF looks scanned. cm-super-minimal is not enough: it leaves the design sizes the CV uses for headings and small print as Type 3 bitmaps fontawesome5 (vendored) The contact icons in the CV header. Debian ships it only inside the 1.7 GB texlive-fonts-extra, so it is vendored as a TeX Live archive in server/docker/vendor/ and unpacked into TEXMFLOCAL. No network access during the build

The image is ~780 MB, almost all of it that toolchain.

docs.title: Run it
docs.text:
docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env ats-strike-server
curl localhost:8080/healthz          # expect "pdflatex": true

It runs as any uid (--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"), needs no volume, and works with a read-only root filesystem as long as /tmp is writable and executable:

docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:exec -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env ats-strike-server

exec on that tmpfs is required: pdflatex writes and then reads back its font cache there. A tmpfs also means a CV session does not survive a restart — mount a volume, or a bucket, at ATS_WORK_DIR if you want it to.

server/compose.yaml does all of the above with the settings already wired:

cp .env.example .env     # then fill in one provider's API key
cd server && docker compose up --build

The published image is on Docker Hub:

docker run -d -p 8080:8080 -e MODEL_API_KEY=... \
  -e MODEL_API_KEY2=... -e MODEL_BASE_URL2=https://api.deepseek.com lmstch/ats-strike:latest

:latest and :x.y.z are pushed by the release workflow, not by hand — see Cutting a release. Pin the version tag if you want the server to stay where the client you handed out expects it.

docs.title: The provider
docs.text:
Three model roles, one provider, one API key. The endpoint is declared once in the [provider] table of resources/models.toml; the key comes from the environment.

MODEL_API_KEY=sk-...
MODEL_BASE_URL=https://dashscope-intl.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1

Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works — OpenAI, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, a local Ollama. Switching providers is replacing those two values; models.toml names the same two variables and does not need to change.

A model that sets use_alternate_provider = 2 calls a second endpoint, from MODEL_API_KEY2 / MODEL_BASE_URL2, instead; 3 uses MODEL_API_KEY3 / MODEL_BASE_URL3, and so on. The shipped six CV steps all use 2, DeepSeek's own API (https://api.deepseek.com): the server builds every role at startup and does not start without those two.

Per-role overrides need no rebuild either — ATS_<ROLE>_<FIELD>, for any key of a role, for DETECT, ANALYSIS, LETTER, JD_EVALUATION, PROFILE_SCORING, FORMAT_SELECTION, CV (the body), DUTIES (the experiences), VALIDATION and HIGHLIGHT:

ATS_CV_MODEL=qwen-max
ATS_CV_TEMPERATURE=0.2
ATS_CV_THINKING=off            # auto | on | off
ATS_CV_REASONING_EFFORT=high   # any string the provider accepts
ATS_CV_API=responses           # chat_completions | responses
ATS_CV_MODEL_PROVIDER=deepseek # standard | deepseek
ATS_CV_EXTRA_BODY={"thinking_budget": 4000}   # JSON; replaces the whole table
ATS_CV_USE_ALTERNATE_PROVIDER=2  # MODEL_API_KEY2 / MODEL_BASE_URL2
ATS_LETTER_TEMPERATURE=        # empty sends no temperature (OpenAI's reasoning models reject one)
ATS_LETTER_EXTRA_BODY={}       # no enable_search, for an endpoint without DashScope's

Nothing checks a combination against what the endpoint supports: what a role declares is what is sent. The comments in models.toml list the known traps.

docs.title: Prompts and the template
docs.text:
The five prompts and resume.tex.jinja ship inside the image. To change them permanently, mount a directory with your versions and set ATS_RESOURCES; anything missing there falls back to the built-in copy. To change them for one request, upload them as parts — that is what the client does when it finds them next to its executable.

docker run -p 8080:8080 --env-file .env \
  -v "$PWD/my-resources:/resources:ro" -e ATS_RESOURCES=/resources \
  ats-strike-server

docs.title: From a checkout
docs.text:
uv sync
uv run ats-strike            # http://localhost:8080
uv run pytest tests/server      # no API key, no network
uv run pytest                   # every package, plus the integration test

The LaTeX-dependent tests skip themselves when pdflatex is absent. Nothing in the suite calls a model: tests/pipeline/pipeline_helpers.py wires a real ModelSelector to a fake HTTP transport, so request assembly, structured output, retries and usage logging are all the production code paths. tests/pipeline/golden/cv_golden.tex pins the whole render — an escaping regression is otherwise invisible until someone reads a bad PDF.

docs.title: Deploying
docs.text:
A CV job runs for minutes after the request that started it has been answered. That is the one thing to plan around.

  • ATS_WORK_DIR is state. Every CV session lives there until the client acknowledges it, or until its last event is older than ATS_SESSION_TTL_DAYS. The default is the system temp directory, which on most container platforms is RAM-backed and empty again after a redeploy. Mount a volume — or a bucket, as server/terraform does on Alibaba Cloud — to have sessions outlive the instance. Each event is a file written once, which a bucket mounted as a folder can do.
  • One process per work root. The job slots and the worker threads are per-process, and a starting process ends every session that has not ended with a 503 — right for its own orphans, wrong for a sibling's live jobs.
  • A CV's stream lasts as long as its job. Every other call returns in seconds; only /v1/cv/render waits on a compile. A platform request timeout has to outlast ATS_REQUEST_BUDGET_SECONDS plus the round in flight; the client reconnects after a cut, but some platforms restart the instance on a timeout.
  • Size for the compiles, not the waiting. Ten jobs in flight is the default; each is mostly idle on the provider — up to ten calls at once, for the steps that score or write one item each — but each also compiles LaTeX once, or a few times when it has to be trimmed.
  • Scaling. A running job lives in the instance that started it: run one instance.
  • Cold starts build an HTTP client per model role and read the prompts. Fast — but the first request also warms the LaTeX font cache in /tmp.

docs.title: Sandboxing
docs.text: A request may supply the LaTeX template, and /v1/cv/render accepts a whole .tex. That is arbitrary LaTeX, so every compile runs with shell escape disabled (-no-shell-escape, shell_escape=f), reads and writes confined to the scratch directory (openin_any=p, openout_any=p), no stdin to block on, a timeout, and its own HOME/TEXMFVAR. The scratch directory is deleted when the request ends, and the scratch path is scrubbed out of any LaTeX log that goes back to a client.

docs.title: In CI
docs.text:
.github/workflows/ci.yml has three jobs. The image one builds with DOCKER_BUILDKIT=0, starts the container with a deliberately invalid provider endpoint, and asserts /healthz reports "pdflatex":true — the image is checked for the toolchain, not for a model.

.github/workflows/release.yml builds it the same way — classic builder, linux/amd64 — and adds one assertion before it pushes: that /healthz reports the version being released. The server reads its version from the installed package metadata, which the image builds with --no-editable, so that check is what proves the number on the Docker Hub tag is the number the container will report.

docs.title: A run, end to end
docs.text: One posting, from the moment you press Ctrl+C on a job ad to the folder that holds the PDF. This is cv clipboard with one server, the default. submit runs the same steps once, for one file, and writes the CV on the main thread before it returns. watch reads postings from a folder and asks only about the CHECK ones — see the client guide. With --server_ver the default still does the detection, the analysis and the letter, and each named server writes its CV on a thread of its own (see several servers).

docs.title: Step by step
docs.text:
1 — The free check runs on your machine. static_jd_guess lives in contracts/ precisely so both sides run the same one: the client uses it before spending a network call, the server before spending a model call. Copying a password or a line of code never reaches the network, and the terminal says so: [clipboard] ✗ not a job description (412 chars, nothing sent).

2 — /healthz before the first real call. A freshly started server (a cold container, a scale-to-zero platform) can take a moment to answer, so the client knocks up to three times, two seconds apart, once per server — not once per call. With -v it narrates the attempts. A server that speaks another protocol is refused there and then.

3 — Detection costs one small model call. POST /v1/jd/detect answers {"is_job_description": true|false}. Why something was rejected is in the server's log for that request, not in the answer — a caller only ever branches on the verdict. A false verdict on a posting you wanted usually means the copy grabbed only part of the page.

4 — Analysis creates the folder, unless the posting was seen before. The analysis comes back as the server wrote it, an opaque JSON object, with its log lines for the folder's log.log. Its company name and job title are what the folder is named after, so the folder cannot exist before the analysis does. First every analysis.json under CV/, discarded/ and working/ is compared with the new one: a posting already applied to, discarded or still in flight is dropped with the earlier folder's path, and nothing is written. Otherwise job_description.txt, analysis.json and approval_status.txt saying PENDING are written at once.

5 — The question is the only thing standing between you and the bill. Everything before it costs one or two small model calls; everything after it costs minutes of the large one. You are asked about every posting, whatever its should_apply says. Answer with the posting URL and it is stored in analysis.json (and in the spreadsheet); y submits without one; n or s files it under discarded/; q stops, and leaves the posting PENDING in working/. --yes answers for you, with the URL the analysis found if it found one.

6 — The CV is written in the background. Saying yes writes APPROVED and queues the folder on every server's queue; each server's CV thread takes one folder at a time, and the clipboard is read again at once, so you read the next posting while the last one's CV is written. Its lines are tagged with the folder's name, and held back while a question is on screen. q between postings lets the CV being written finish; the approved ones still queued stay in working/.

7 — The CV job is a session the client follows. POST /v1/cv sends the server folder (the pack), the posting with what that server stored for it before (the job), and its [settings], and returns 202 at once, under a session id that is the SHA-256 of the posting's text. The client then reads the session's events as the server writes them: each new status, printed; with -v, each step's detail too, and every log line — one per model call, with its cost. Every store item is kept as it arrives: each step's result in the server's subfolder (v11/steps/…, v11/cv.json, v11/cv.tex), each log line in log.log, the PDF at the top of the folder. The last log line is what the whole run cost; once done arrives, everything is written, and the client acknowledges the session and the server deletes it.

If the connection drops, the client opens the stream again from the last event it got. If the client dies mid-job, the job does not: the server keeps writing the session. Run the same posting again and the server answers with the session it already has — replayed from the start, nothing paid twice. --new drops it and writes the CV again.

8 — The next start picks up where this one stopped. Anything left in working/ is offered back at startup: resume, clean or quit. Resume sends each folder where its own files say: APPROVED to the CV threads, PENDING to you before anything new is read. A folder that already holds a server's cv.json sends it with the job, and that server renders it instead of writing a new CV — one LaTeX compile, no model call.

9 — Failure is filed, not printed and lost. A CV job that fails ends its session with an error event — the cause, after the log line saying what the attempts cost — and everything the server logged for it is already in log.log; the client acknowledges the session. When no server wrote its CV, the job moves to error/; when another did, it is delivered and the failure stays in log.log and in the exit code. Any other call that fails carries a request_id, written into the log and printed: the server's own log has that request's lines under it.

10 — The spreadsheet is bookkeeping, never a reason to fail. A locked or broken applications.xlsx becomes a warning line in log.log; the CV was paid for and stays delivered.
